points.title: Computer network
points.must: Definition: two or more devices connected (cable or wireless) to communicate and share resources; contrast with a standalone computer.
points.model: Computer network = two or more computers or devices connected together (by cable or wirelessly) so that they can communicate and share resources — data, files, printers, software and an Internet connection. Standalone computer = not connected to any network; uses only its own storage, software and peripherals.

points.title: Node
points.must: Definition of a node with examples of devices.
points.model: Node = any device connected to a network that can send or receive data, e.g. computer, laptop, phone, printer, server, switch, router.

points.title: Advantages of networking
points.must: At least four advantages, each with a short reason/example.
points.model: 1) Share hardware — one printer/scanner for many users (saves cost). 2) Share one Internet connection. 3) Share files and data — everyone uses the same up-to-date copy, e.g. one patient database in a clinic. 4) Share/install software centrally; updates from one place. 5) Communication — e-mail, messaging, video calls. 6) Log on at any computer and see your own files. 7) Central management, security and automatic backup.

points.title: Disadvantages of networking
points.model: 1) Cost of cables, switches, routers, servers and a network manager. 2) Security risks — malware can spread to all computers; hackers can reach many users' data. 3) If a key device (server/switch) fails, many users are affected. 4) Network can become congested and slow with heavy traffic. 5) Needs specialist maintenance.

points.title: How data moves: NIC, media, packets, protocols
points.must: NIC and MAC address, transmission medium, data split into packets with addresses, protocols as rules.
points.model: Each node has a network interface card (NIC) that turns data into signals; each NIC has a unique MAC address. Signals travel along a transmission medium (copper cable, fibre-optic, radio/Wi-Fi). Data is split into packets carrying sender and receiver addresses. Protocols = rules for formatting, addressing and sending data (Ethernet in a LAN, TCP/IP on the Internet).

points.title: Switch vs router
points.must: Switch joins devices inside one network; router joins a network to other networks (LAN to WAN/Internet).
points.model: Switch = connects devices inside one network (LAN) and passes data to the addressed device. Router = connects one network to other networks (LAN to a WAN or the Internet) and forwards packets towards their destination.

points.title: LAN
points.must: Definition in exam wording with an example.
points.model: LAN (Local Area Network) = a network covering a small geographical area such as one building or site (school, office, home), usually owned and managed by one organisation. Example: the school computer network.

points.title: WAN
points.must: Definition in exam wording: large area, connects LANs, leased links; example.
points.model: WAN (Wide Area Network) = a network covering a large geographical area (cities, countries, the world), usually connecting LANs together using links leased/rented from telecommunications companies. Examples: a bank linking its branches across Kazakhstan; the Internet.

points.title: The Internet as the largest WAN
points.must: Internet = global network of networks, no single owner, common protocols TCP/IP.
points.model: The Internet is the largest WAN: a global network of interconnected networks (LANs and WANs of ISPs, companies, universities) with no single owner, all using the TCP/IP protocols. A home router joins the home LAN to the ISP and so to the Internet.

points.title: Other network sizes
points.must: PAN, WLAN, MAN with area and example, in order of size.
points.model: PAN — a few metres around one person, e.g. phone + earbuds + smartwatch by Bluetooth. LAN — a building/site. WLAN — a LAN using Wi-Fi radio waves instead of cables, e.g. home Wi-Fi. MAN — one city, e.g. city network of libraries/CCTV. WAN — countries/the world.

points.title: LAN vs WAN: area, ownership, cost
points.must: Comparison with both sides and reasons for area, ownership and cost.
points.model: A LAN covers a small geographical area (one site), whereas a WAN covers a large area (countries). A LAN is owned by one organisation with its own cables, whereas a WAN uses links leased from telecom companies (cannot lay cables across public land). A LAN is cheap to set up with no rental, whereas a WAN is expensive — equipment plus monthly rental.

points.title: LAN vs WAN: speed, latency, errors
points.must: Bandwidth and latency defined; LAN higher bandwidth, lower latency, fewer errors, with reasons.
points.model: Bandwidth = amount of data sent per second. Latency = delay before data arrives. A LAN has high bandwidth (1–10 Gbit/s) and very low latency, whereas a WAN usually has lower bandwidth per user and higher latency, because data travels further and passes through many routers. A LAN has few errors, whereas a WAN has more errors from long links and interference.

points.title: LAN vs WAN: media and security
points.must: Typical media for each; security difference and VPN/encryption.
points.model: LAN media: twisted-pair Ethernet cable, Wi-Fi, short fibre. WAN media: fibre-optic (incl. undersea), telephone lines, microwave, satellite. A LAN is easier to secure because access is physically controlled, whereas WAN data crosses other companies' links and must be encrypted (e.g. VPN).

points.title: Worked comparison: school vs bank
points.must: The school (LAN) and bank branches across Kazakhstan (WAN) example with the compared points.
points.model: School in one building = LAN: owned by the school, 1 Gbit/s, almost no delay, paid once for cables. Bank with 60 branches across Kazakhstan = WAN: each branch LAN joined by routers to leased fibre/satellite links, monthly rental, lower bandwidth per branch, more delay, traffic encrypted in a VPN.
